card: Hegel spent 9 to 11 on a third visit to the Esterhazy gallery. Prince Esterhazy, told that a Berlin professor was there, had a valet show Hegel everything, including the private cabinet. Hegel then lunched at an inn with Professor Sonnleitner, director of the antiquities cabinet, and a professor from Padua. In the evening he saw Rossini's Corradino.
X: Now this morning, for the third time, out to the Esterházy Collection; treasures to be admired without end! — one really cannot get enough of them. — The finest pieces are in the Prince’s private room, a garden room in the pavilion — next to the castle, where the great gallery is; the Prince was in this room and, as he heard me walking around, he asked who it was? — since it was not one of the public days; — he was pleased to hear that it was a Berlin professor who had already come for the third time and ordered the valet to show me everything, and as he soon drove off, I was also able to see the magnificent pieces of the cabinet once more — what a living room! — This Prince can travel a few miles from Vienna on his own land and property right up to the Turkish border. — Stayed there from 9 to 11 o’clock, — then — half an hour to go home, — changed clothes — to the Antiquities Cabinet, whose director, Prof. Sonnleitner, had invited me — he is unmarried — to lunch with him at an inn with a professor from Padua — a very learned and amiable man. We scholars are immediately much more at home with one another than with bankers, for example. — Then some walks in the city, — finally also to the Italian Opera and, as I had so much wished, Corradino il cuor di ferro, — which was melted and softened by the charming Dardanelli; — how sweetly she sang — and how David sang again with her! I did not contradict a man with whom I had entered into conversation at dinner last evening, who even went so far as to claim that Rossini’s music is music for the heart.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with culture, and I am somewhat exhausted by the excess of it. I spent three hours today in the Esterhazy gallery. The Prince, hearing a professor from Berlin had arrived, insisted I see the private cabinet. It is a magnificent collection, though I found myself thinking of how such private hoarding contrasts with the public spirit of a state.

I dined with Professor Sonnleitner and a man from Padua. We spoke of antiquities, but mostly of the wine, which was excellent. In the evening, I attended Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is dazzling, full of that Italian lightness, though I confess I found the drama somewhat thin. It moves the senses, certainly, but does it move the spirit?

I am tired but content. Think of me by the fire in Berlin.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: Having left Paris, Hegel was in Brussels, staying at the house of his friend van Ghert. Madame van Ghert cut a quill pen for him, and he had a letter from his wife fetched from the post office.
X: Also Brussels! in the house of my friend Mr. van Ghert)) and with a quill that Mde van Ghert has just cut for me, and indeed in a trice, with a single press. — You see hereby that it has become serious, to renounce Paris, — which you, in your letter, which I have just had fetched from the post, — wanted to doubt would happen so soon...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Brussels this evening, exhausted but in good spirits. I am staying at the house of my friend Van Ghert, whose hospitality is most welcome. Madame Van Ghert was kind enough to cut a fresh quill for me, a small gesture that made the room feel less like an inn and more like home.

I have received your letter from the post office, which I have read with great pleasure. It is a comfort to hear of the household’s peace while I am away. The journey has been steady, though the fatigue accumulates. I find myself thinking of our sons and the quiet order of our Berlin home more than usual.

I shall not stay long. The road calls, and I must continue my observations of this part of the world. I hope this letter finds you well and that the boys are behaving as they should.

Your loving Georg

card: Hegel spent the day in Cologne, looking at the Rhine and the many large two-masted vessels on it, and visiting several churches. For Sunday morning he planned to attend a mass with music in the cathedral, probably with the young Counts Stolberg and their longtime tutor, Dean Kellermann, and to leave for Aachen that afternoon.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The evening light here is peculiar, catching the Rhine in a way that makes one forget the hours. I spent the day among the great two-masted vessels, their sails furled against the quiet water, and wandered through the churches. The stone here holds a weight that speaks of centuries, not just the present moment.

I am to attend the cathedral mass tomorrow morning. The music, I am told, is worthy of the occasion. I shall be accompanied by the young Counts Stolberg and their tutor, Dean Kellermann. We must depart for Aachen this afternoon, so the day is already moving us forward.

Think of me as I stand here, watching the river flow toward the sea. It is a fine, if tired, traveler’s view. Give my regards to the boys. I hope the snuff I purchased in Bonn suits your father.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: This is my day's work, — of course, I have also seen the Rhine, the endless row of large two-masted ships on it, and a few more churches. Tomorrow morning, Sunday — probably in the company of the young Counts of Stolberg and Dean Kellermann, their teacher for many years, who was present at Stolberg's death — I will still see the cathedral with a musical mass and other things, and then depart for Aachen tomorrow afternoon.

card: The previous evening's programme had ended with the first act of a ballet in which the German dancer Eberle appeared. This morning Hegel went early to the imperial library to view works by Raphael and Marcantonio. Viennese collections were open free on fixed days, the library daily; he tipped the attendants at each visit. The weather cleared in the afternoon.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The morning was bright, and I spent it in the Imperial Library. I had hoped to see more, but I lingered over the Raphael and the Marcantonios. They are masterpieces, truly. I left a small tip for the attendant; it is the only way to keep the doors open and the eyes off one’s back. I find that in Vienna, as everywhere, a little coin smooths the path.

Yesterday’s ballet was a spectacle, though I confess I found the German dancer Eberle less convincing than the critics did. The weather has finally cleared, and the air feels lighter. I am tired, as one always is after a day of looking at other men’s genius, but my spirits are good. I am thinking of you and the boys constantly. Do not worry about me; I am eating well, and the wine here is not half bad.

I shall write again soon.

Your affectionate,
Georg
Y: Current and blessed, it penetrates and liberates every situation! Ask the Milder whether it is not so; — she herself, in happy; not Rossini’s music, is this, for her tone, sound, and action are from the house and from the beginning out of passion and soulful penetration, — You yourself also feel this, when in re-echoes or even only in memory this fullness re-echoes in you, lives on, and storms on. — It would still be worth mentioning that finally the first act of yesterday’s ballet was performed; Eberle, a German, danced excellently, though not quite the Italian manner of a Torelli, who with her admirable manners and even more her Roman physiognomy, gave me also an idea of Italian dancing. — But now from these profane observations and plays of the 5th Oct.... The weather has cleared up again this afternoon; certainly the Berliner Dittmar has predicted this, — for here first and in the local newspapers I see how much this prophet here, — where his fatherland is not, — counts; for which reason I also did not stay in Swabia, but went over Nuremberg to Berlin. To return to my dry historical relation, — this morning early to the Imperial and Royal Library, having been with Raphael and Marc Anton. What soulful delicacy, what Unica! Along with this also again a prosaic remark: — here one sees on certain days (in the Imperial and Royal Library every day) all the treasures of artistic genius — free of charge; to the serving attendants one gives perhaps a tip and I have always, even when it was not necessary, given tips, to do honor at least to the royal Prussian professorship. On the other hand, the Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness is notorious here and in the whole world! — and I, royal Professor publ. ordin. at the royal university in Berlin (and indeed Professor of the subject, namely of Philosophy, as the

card: In Aachen Hegel sat in Charlemagne's coronation chair, shown by the sexton. He spent three hours in the morning and three in the afternoon viewing Bettendorf's painting collection, with Bettendorf himself present, then walked toward Burtscheid and took a sulphur bath. Leaving by coach early Tuesday, he reached Liège around five and stayed overnight with one fellow passenger.
X: But they were covered with gold leaf, which had engraved stories on it, of which some pieces are still preserved. On this throne, 300 years after his death, Karl was found sitting, I believe, by Emperor Friedrich, with the imperial regalia put on him, the crown on his head, the scepter in one hand, and the orb in the other; these items were added to the Imperial Regalia and his bones were interred. I sat on this throne, on which 32 emperors had been crowned, as the sacristan assured me, just as well as anyone else, and the whole satisfaction is that one has sat on it. — But the main thing was that I saw the collection of Mr. Bettendorf (which is now being sold individually) for 3 hours in the morning and likewise in the afternoon, and he had the kindness to keep me company himself. In regard to Old German art, it is the counterpart to the Boisseree collection; both combined, as both gentlemen intended — purchased by the King — would represent the most magnificent thing in this sphere of art. Mr. Bettendorf does not have such large and distinguished van Eycks as Boisseree, but his Hemlings, one picture in particular, are at least as excellent as the Boisseree ones. Some of the figures in the Boisseree Hemlings, especially the Jew gathering manna, is exactly the same one who cuts the Paschal lamb on the Bettendorf picture. — But one picture by a Roger is the highest thing one can see; every particularity — some dryness that one would wish to remove even from the most excellent Eyck works — has completely disappeared here; it is as magnificently Italian as it is Netherlandish. A jewel is likewise a picture — a Deposition from the Cross with many figures, drawn by Raphael and painted by Albrecht Dürer, what loveliness, what beauty!! — A woman with a child — attributed by some to Michelangelo — is an infinitely great painting. But above all, a night by Correggio! — just as I called the Dresden one the day of Correggio, so this is the true night. What a picture! The light emanating equally from the child — Mary is dearer to me here than in the Dresden one, and she, like the surroundings in this one, smiles — everything is also cheerful — but more serious, and the darkness, as in the Correggio pictures in Sanssouci, of the later manner of this master — of the highest excellence. In the evening I still took a walk towards Burtscheid, and since the famous bath is in Aachen, I took a bath: it is hot! and full of sulphur smell. — On Tuesday morning at 7 o'clock we left Aachen and arrived in Liège around 5 o'clock; the road goes up hill, down hill, mostly on a ridge, with deeper valleys on both sides, everything green, intersected by innumerable hedges and rows of trees. Towards Liège one gets views into the beautiful Meuse valley; I was very tempted to travel from Liège up the Meuse valley via Namur to here — but I would have spent nearly two days longer, because of the curse of the carriages, and part of the journey would have been made at night, when no one sees anything. In Liège I stayed overnight with one of the travelers; the carriage on which we had arrived went straight on; among the traveling party there was just again such a flat, chatty German — a Würzburger, who also wants to be an Englishman — annoying people, as I had had one in every carriage party so far. My
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The day has been a strange mix of history and hygiene. Here in Aachen, the sexton actually let me sit in Charlemagne’s own coronation chair. It was a curious sensation; one feels the weight of the state not as an abstraction, but as a physical seat. I spent the whole day with Bettendorf, examining his paintings until the light failed, and then walked out to Burtscheid for a sulphur bath. It is a strange remedy, but the water is hot and the air is sharp.

I have since traveled to Liège, arriving late this evening. I am staying with a fellow passenger for the night. The journey is uneventful, but the mind is full. I miss the quiet of Berlin and your company. I shall continue north tomorrow. Give my love to the boys.

Yours,
G. W. F. Hegel

card: With his luggage already sent off through a shipping firm, Hegel spent the evening of the emperor's name day at the Italian opera. Twenty-nine singers of the Italian company, among them Fodor, Dardanelli, David, Donzelli, Rubini and Lablache, sang the anthem in unison. Rain ruled out illuminations. The house was full, and a German cast premiered an Auber opera.
X:
My dearest Marie,

Vienna is magnificent, even in the rain. The Emperor’s name day was marked by a full house at the Italian Opera. We sat through twenty-nine singers—Fodor, Rubini, among them—shouting the anthem in unison. It was a spectacle of noise rather than subtlety. The rain prevented the usual illuminations, so we missed the visual display, but the German premiere of Auber’s opera was a pleasant surprise. The crowd was spirited, if a bit loud.

I have already sent my luggage off ahead of me. I feel light, ready to move on. Do not worry about the small things here; I am well. I miss your quiet presence in Berlin, but this travel has a certain invigorating quality. I hope the boys are well-behaved and that your health is sound. I shall write again soon from Prague.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.
Y: Still Vienna! My effects have already been handed over to the shipping agent, — some additions, — the subtractions belong to the travel expenses; — these, however, are no heathen money, but everything was spent on Christians and used for me — also a good Christian. Now, after the completion of such business, to — where? To the Italian Theatre! To — first, the popular song — as today on St. Francis’s Day. — The rainy weather, however, did not allow illuminations to appear, which otherwise would have been perhaps the only celebration of this day; I could learn nothing of any further fuss. I also celebrated this day by listening to the aforementioned song, performed on one side by Mrs. Fodor à la tête, then Dardanelli and so on, 13 in number, and on the other side by Signor David à la tête, Donzelli, also Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco etc., 16 men high — although unison, but without solos, variations. So for such means not enough action, — the men in black, the ladies in white satin! The house was this time packed full, probably for Francis’s Day, also for the sake of the German Opera, which was given for the first time today, — French music performed by Germans and German women. On the one hand, because of the packed full house, I had for the first time the opportunity to see very many, i.e., several pretty ladies, and on the other hand I could notice more of the Viennese ladies on my part, because I did not have to see and hear Italians and Italian women on the stage. I also pass from that to the German Opera, i.e., the French charming music by Auber, performed by German throats! In the last act, passion comes into the voices through a French coup, and here they let themselves go, but earlier the soul of the song only comes to peeping and longing and being small-voiced. — But with the Italians there is immediately longing-free sound, and the metal of the nature from the first moment on, ignited and in motion; the first sound is freedom and passion, — the first tone immediately goes with free breast and soul blessed into the fray! — the divine Furore is from the start melodic

card: Hegel reached Amsterdam shortly after noon and went directly to Dr. Besseling, to whom Mr. van Ghert had recommended him. Afterwards he visited the picture gallery, which holds paintings by Rembrandt measuring 15 to 20 feet across and 12 feet high. He did not get through the whole collection that day.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I am settled here in Amsterdam, having arrived shortly after noon. I went straight to Dr. Besseling’s, where Mr. van Ghert’s recommendation opened the door. It is a house of order, which I appreciate after the chaos of travel.

I spent the afternoon in the picture gallery. I confess I was struck dumb before a Rembrandt—fifteen to twenty feet across, twelve high. It is not mere decoration; it is the spirit of the age made visible, the individual soul expanded into the universal. I did not finish the collection, but I have seen enough to know that art here speaks the language of freedom we have only begun to articulate in our own land.

The light in the evening is distinct, grey and clear. I miss the warmth of your hearth and the noise of the boys. Write soon.

Your G. W. F.
Y: Arrived here in Amsterdam at 12:07 o'clock, immediately went to Dr. Besseling, to whom I had been recommended by Mr. van Ghert — a very obliging man — then to the painting gallery, — here are works by Rembrandt, 15 to 20 feet wide, 12 feet high, I have not yet seen everything.

card: Hegel stayed mostly indoors in Koblenz, where Councillor Lange was absent, then on Wednesday afternoon took a boat to Neuwied and saw the Moravian Sisters' House. Next morning he boarded the Rhine passenger boat in rain, stopped at Linz to see a painting Schulze had recommended in a hilltop church, and at Bonn called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Cologne, tired but content. The journey has been a mix of rain and reflection. In Koblenz, I waited out the absence of Councillor Lange, which gave me time to sit with my thoughts. Yesterday, I took the boat to Neuwied to visit the Moravian Sisters. Their quiet devotion is striking; one sees the ethical life in its simplest, most earnest form.

This morning, the rain was heavy as I boarded the Rhine steamer. I stopped at Linz to view a painting in a hilltop church, as Schulze advised. It was worth the climb. In Bonn, I called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther. We spoke, and the wine was good.

I think of you and the boys here in Berlin. The river moves on, and so do I, but my heart remains with you. Do not worry about my health; the change of air is doing me good. I shall write again soon.

Your loving,
G. W. F. Hegel
Y: So I would have been happy to have arrived in the venerable Imperial City of Cologne.... In Coblenz, where my last letter ends, I spent the afternoon and the following morning mostly resting at home — the Consistory Councillor Lange, to whom Schulze had addressed me, was not present, — and in indecision about the weather I let the express coaches, steam packets, and other opportunities pass by; but on Wednesday afternoon it cleared up; I took a boat and went to Neuwied on the beautiful Rhine; I saw the Moravian Brethren' house; — it became too dark to go into the Prince's Brazilian collection. The most beautiful thing was the evening — beautiful moonlight shone over the Rhine, which flowed past my windows; owls, which I had never heard speak in my life, made music in it, — in the morning after 8 o'clock onto the steam packet, an improved market boat. — At first one could be somewhat on the deck, but then it became windy, cold, rainy, finally continuous, heavy, cold rain. The company was thus confined in the cabin, and there were also students in it, who were making their Rhine journey, so with the knapsack, covered with green oilcloth and with a boot sticking out on each side of it, wide new straps, — everything in order, also white, or rather yellow straw hats. So I, although with somewhat more ballast than they, also made my Rhine journey, but therefore saw less, and was inferior to them in that I could not gain the proud consciousness of making a Rhine journey. Already the rainy weather in Coblenz, — above all this Rhine journeying, had spoiled my travel, and if it had not been so far home to you, above all if I had not been afraid of the post coaches, I would have quickly arrived at your place. I travel in general only out of duty and obligation, and would have a hundred times more satisfaction and pleasure if I could divide my time between my studies and you. If you ever come with me to this Rhine, I will lead you differently; on the water one sees neither the Rhine nor the country, — the former not, for one does not see it flowing through the fields and hills, one does not have it as a part of the picture before one, which is its truly beautiful position or flow — nor the country, for one sees only the banks, their boundaries and notices at most that it might be beautiful behind them. — In Linz we went ashore, where I saw the picture recommended by my friend Privy Councillor Schulze, and that in a high-situated church, from where one overlooks the Rhine and the beautiful country. — In abominable rain we went ashore in Bonn. Here I looked for Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther), whom you know from Thibaut, — with the former, who through union in prayer with Prince Hohenlohe?) has been healed for a year of a six-year eye ailment of the kind like Jacobi's, only much worse — and is now perfectly healthy, I got along very well, and we, for the time being, were very satisfied with each other. Walther also pleased me, who remembers you with very heartfelt remembrance, and sends you friendly greetings. — This encounter refreshed me again. To this was added the clearing up of the weather, and so I set out yesterday afternoon in a better disposition.... Bonn is hawkerish, very narrow-streeted, but the surroundings, view, botanical garden — beautiful, very beautiful, but I am still rather in Berlin.

card: Leaving Cousin in Brussels, Hegel took the diligence to Ghent on Friday morning and viewed the parts of the van Eyck altarpiece kept there. At 2 p.m. he boarded a horse-drawn canal barge, where passengers read or played whist in the cabin, and reached Bruges at 8 p.m.
X: On Friday morning I set out — my cousin remained in Brussels — on the diligence to Ghent, saw what could be seen of the Eyck painting there (of which we have the fine pieces in Berlin), and at 2 o’clock boarded the barge to Bruges on the canal (— it is drawn by horses; in the cabin one reads, plays whist, and so on); at 8 o’clock in the evening I arrived. Ghent has 70,000 inhabitants, Bruges 33,000 — in the exterior of the latter, the peculiar Dutch style of building is entirely preserved, which is already blurred and modernized in Ghent, and even more so in Brussels.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The heat was stifling, but the journey to Bruges has been agreeable enough. I arrived at eight after boarding a canal barge at two. The cabin was pleasantly crowded; passengers read the newspapers or played whist with a fervor that reminded me of our own parlour games. I confess I watched the cards with interest, though I did not join in.

Earlier, in Ghent, I viewed the fragments of the van Eyck altarpiece. The detail is astonishing, a testament to a different kind of spirit. But I find myself thinking less of art and more of the slow, inevitable movement of the state. These canals, these barges, they are not just transport; they are the veins of a commercial order that grows, not as a product of arbitrary will, but as the actuality of the ethical idea.

The air in Bruges is cooler. I hope this letter finds you and the boys well in Berlin. I miss your company and the quiet of our home.

Yours,
G.W.F.

card: Hegel left Kassel by stagecoach on Saturday afternoon; the Englishman he had been travelling with stayed behind. Six passengers rode inside, three to a seat. Hegel sat facing backwards, opposite a student from Göttingen who held on to the rear seat marked number one throughout. The coach soon reached the river Lahn and followed it.
X: Now I would have to continue my travel description. — I departed from Cassel on Saturday afternoon — my Englishman remained there, and I found myself from then on among entirely German countrymen, quite in the national spirit — and missed my beautiful, free Englishman all the more. — We were six (three on each seat), I was facing backwards — a student from Göttingen had and kept his seat No. 1 in the back, opposite me, unmoved —, we sat tightly, it was not for the best. — We soon reached the Lahn, and now followed this river constantly; beautiful, fertile
Y:
My dearest Marie,

We arrived in Koblenz this evening, the heat finally broken by the river. The journey from Kassel was an exercise in endurance. I was forced to sit facing backward, opposite a Göttingen student who clung to the rear seat with a tenacity that bordered on the absurd. The other passengers were a motley crew; one Englishman abandoned us at the last moment, leaving us with the full weight of six souls in a cramped interior.

I confess I found the backward view of the Lahn’s banks strangely comforting, a constant reminder that progress often requires looking at what has just passed. The river followed the coach faithfully, a mirror to our own restless movement. I am tired, but the wine here is good. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, where the air is still. Do not worry; I am merely traversing, not arriving.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: At 10 a.m. Hegel drove with Raumer and his party to Saint-Denis, whose cathedral, burial place of the French kings, was still draped in black from a funeral service, and on to Montmorency. There he rode a donkey to the Hermitage, where Rousseau once lived, and climbed the heights above the town, with Paris and Montmartre in view.
X: I wrote the above yesterday morning — at 10 o’clock I drove with Raumer and his company to St. Denis and Montmoreney. There is the famous cathedral, the burial place of the Kings of France, — it was still hung with black inside from a funeral service the previous day — in Montmoreney there is an estate, called the Hermitage, where Rousseau lived for a time?), and therefore — there are many small relics (there), also a rose bush that he planted — it is frequently visited in a pilgrim-like manner and on donkeys — (also by me with such eagerness) — . Montmoreney lies high and one ascends the higher heights behind it, — one has Paris at a distance of two hours, Montmartre and the large, rich plain dotted with villages and country houses before one. — It is beautiful around Paris, fertile, varied, — no wonder that so much life is lived in the country. This evening I am going to the Italian Opera to hear the Pesaroni — highly praised — in the morning still to the Gallery in the Louvre.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The air here is sharp, and the light on the Seine tonight is unlike anything we have seen in Berlin. I have been to Saint-Denis and Montmorency. The cathedral at Saint-Denis is draped in black for a recent funeral; it is a heavy, solemn sight, reminding one that even kings are subject to the march of history. From Montmorency, I rode a donkey to Rousseau’s Hermitage. It is a modest place, but the view from the heights above the town is commanding. I could see all of Paris, with Montmartre rising in the distance. It struck me how the capital looks from here—not as a city of noise, but as a vast, living organism of the spirit. The journey has been tiring, but the mind is refreshed. I miss your presence and the comfort of our home. Do not worry about me; I am well, if a little dusty. Write soon.

Your loving
G.W.F.

card: Heavy rain began overnight and lasted through Sunday into the next morning. Hegel rested on Sunday morning; after lunch, despite the rain, he took a carriage to the Augarten and on to Nussdorf. Along the road he saw a large pear tree, its fruit already harvested, in blossom again, and he enclosed two of its blossoms in his letter.
X: But now it began to rain terribly at night, all through Sunday and still this morning! What is this to become! Yet one must not give up hope. On Sunday morning I was glad that it was raining so hard—I had to rest once— but after dinner I had myself driven to the Augarten and to Nußdorf, despite the weather, on the way to which I saw a pear tree, as large as a pear tree can be, covered with blossoms; it has already borne fruit; I enclose here a little blossom, one for you, the other for those who themselves have blossomed from this land, as a sign of how greatly I recognize and value the excellence of such soil. — How the Augarten and Nußdorf are, I have provisionally gathered from this and found them very beautiful...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The rain here is relentless, turning the streets into rivers, but I could not rest. After lunch, I hired a carriage to Nussdorf despite the weather. The air was thick and heavy, yet I felt a strange lightness. On the road, I saw a large pear tree, its fruit long since harvested, yet it was in full blossom again. It seemed absurd, a defiance of the natural order, but there was a certain stubborn vitality in it. I enclosed two of the blossoms in this letter for you. They are not beautiful, but they are a sign that life persists even when it seems out of place or out of season.

I think of you and the boys often. The journey is wearying, but the mind is active. I hope the news finds you well. I shall write again soon.

Yours,
Georg Wilhelm

card: Hegel arrived in Kassel at 11 in the morning and spent the rest of the morning and the afternoon walking about the town. In the evening he sat down to write his wife an account of the journey so far.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I have reached Kassel, arriving just after eleven. The morning was warm, so I spent it wandering the streets and the gardens, letting my thoughts settle after the journey. The town is pleasant enough, though it lacks the bustle of Berlin. I sat in a quiet corner of the Hofgarten for some time, watching the light change, and found myself reflecting on the peculiar stillness of provincial life here. It is a sharp contrast to the intellectual ferment we know at home.

I hope the boys are well-behaved and that your health is steady. I miss our evenings and the comfort of our library. I shall try to rest well tonight, for we must continue our route tomorrow. Do not worry; the roads are good, and I am in high spirits. Give my love to Karl and Immanuel, and tell them their father is thinking of them as he watches the stars come out over the palace.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.
Y: I also arrived in Cassel happily this morning at 11 o'clock, and after having walked about a great deal both in the morning and afternoon, I intend to spend this evening with you, my dear, and with the account of my life and travels up to now.... My journey is not progressing as quickly as I initially intended. It has gone reasonably well for me so far, and for people who have money and stick to the main road, the world is in good condition; — however, it also requires that they have good news from your family; I have departed reassured regarding you; but I cannot be entirely free of worry, and in any case I set out on the road with great reluctance, and I am really only traveling on because I am already on the journey and am supposed to be.

card: Hegel travelled on to Giessen, where he spent time with the philosophy professors of Giessen and Marburg and an associate professor of theology; the Giessen professor took them out for wine. Travellers bound for Frankfurt parted from the group there. Hegel and a Jewish schoolteacher continued together along the Lahn, passing Weilburg, a former princely residence.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The wine in Giessen was excellent, and the company of my colleagues there most lively. We argued over the finer points of logic until the candles burned low, and I must confess I enjoyed the vigorous debate. It is a pleasure to see the spirit of inquiry still alive in these universities.

We have left the main party and are now travelling along the Lahn with a schoolteacher, a man of considerable learning. We passed Weilburg this afternoon; the old princely residence stands quiet against the river, a reminder that power, like thought, must be grounded in its own history to endure. The air is crisp, and the pace is gentle. I am well rested and in good spirits. Do not worry for me; the journey is less a burden than a change of air. I look forward to returning to our study in Berlin to continue our work.

Your devoted husband,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Then we went to Giessen, a pleasant city and surroundings, with two nice castles in the neighborhood. Here I was with three confreres: the Giessen professor of philosophy—Snell?—the Marburg professor of the same, Creuzer?, a cousin of the Heidelberg one—and an extraordinary professor of theology, a man of striving, insight, and cultivation. But how insipid those my nearer confreres had been, I had to overlook, as the Giessen one immediately led us to wine and treated us with very good vintage. In Giessen was the parting point for those who went to Frankfurt, among whom, as we had agreed at the start, I was not, all the less as I would otherwise have spent longer in the company up to now. My young teaching colleague, the Israelite, however, stuck with me; we followed the Lahn. Weilburg has a romantic location, a beautiful, vegetation-rich, narrow valley, pleasant bends of the Lahn—and also, as a former princely residence, nice houses.

card: Hegel spent two afternoon hours at the Belvedere, then saw Rossini's Barber of Seville with Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Rosina, Ambrogi as Bartolo and the newcomer de Franco. The audience applauded entrances and passages, and kept clapping after scenes until singers returned. He read a theatre paper's notice on the company. The Partheys, at his urging, attended every performance.
X: In the afternoon I spent a few more hours at the Belvedere and then attended Rossini's Figaro. What a Figaro Lablache is! What a Rosine Mde Fodor is! She is a perfect singer; what beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing! And the excellent Lablache, what a bass! And how cheerful and freely comic, with nothing low or vulgar anywhere. When the entire chorus sings together, and the orchestra likewise rushes in fortissimo with all its might, it sounds most certainly as if he were singing solo, and this entirely without strain, without shouting, without a screaming tone. Ambrogi was also very good again as Dr. Bartolo, and then there was a new singer, de Franco. It is a whole hedge, partly of the most excellent, partly of flawless excellence. But what a part we the public take! Three to four actors are applauded each time at their first appearance, then every passage is applauded—or bravo! bravi! is called out, then after each scene they are immoderately applauded, the singer thanks and goes off, but the applauding continues with sustained strength, so that he or she is not merely clapped, but rather clapped out. At the end of the piece, however, no calling out or set phrases take place. So, repeated Party and others, one cannot see the Figaro performed anywhere else in Italy. I read today in a Viennese theater sheet that the most experienced are of one opinion that, according to their longest memory, no such Italian company has been in Vienna for 50 years, and certainly will not come again for the next 50 years. The Party people, after I had argued them into it, naturally did not miss a single performance and were collectively most delighted, even though they disparaged the Rossinian music, which sometimes also makes me bored as music.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The light here in Vienna is peculiar, softening the edges of things. I spent the afternoon at the Belvedere; the paintings do not shout, but they hold a quiet dignity that speaks to the mind without demanding it.

Tonight, however, the mind was overwhelmed by the senses. I attended Rossini’s *Barber of Seville*. The Partheys, as I urged them, were there to share the experience. Lablache’s Figaro is a marvel of wit, and the company’s energy is infectious. The audience’s applause was not merely polite; it was a collective affirmation of the joy on stage, breaking the usual reserve of the Viennese. It reminded me that art, at its height, is the liberation of spirit through form.

I am tired but happy. The journey is long, but such moments make the miles worthwhile. Think of me as I sit here, writing by candlelight, longing for our table in Berlin.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

card: Hegel arrived in Metz after 3 p.m. and stayed the night. He reserved a front coupé seat on the diligence to Paris. Before the meal he walked through the town, seeing the cathedral from outside and the Moselle valley from the ramparts. Afterwards he attended the theatre, where garrison officers filled most seats, for a play and a vaudeville.
X: At this moment, after 3 p.m., I arrive here; I could immediately depart for Paris at 5 o'clock; but according to my usual system, I intend to rest again. So I am, in fact, in France! Evening. I have already had myself registered in the Lafitte diligence in the Coupé; that is the front compartment of the carriage; there are three boxes one behind the other; the middle one is called l'interieur and the rear one Cabriolet; the Coupé has 3 seats side by side, facing forward, and is closed with windows, not open, like the so-called Cabriolets on our express post coaches. Before dinner I briefly viewed the city somewhat, the cathedral from the outside and especially the view from a part of the rampart, which is most charming; the valley, through which the Moselle flows, bounded by gentle hills, wider, richer in buildings and villages, and more attractive than the surroundings of Dresden. Since Metz is a significant fortress, the garrison is numerous. After dinner I went to the theater, which was full of officers; hardly a dozen women and civilians; List against List, — also in Germany on the theater, — and then a Vaudeville, all nonsensical — and very cold — stuff, but played and spoken with such liveliness that I understood hardly a word, especially from the wretched singing.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Metz this afternoon, the light already softening on the Moselle. I walked the ramparts to catch the valley below, a stillness that suits the end of a day’s labor. The cathedral looms from outside, imposing but distant; I have no time to enter its mysteries tonight, only to observe its stone.

Dinner was decent, though I found the company at the theatre rather tedious. It was crowded with garrison officers, their laughter loud and their attention short. They watched a vaudeville with a distraction that reminded me of students who have not yet learned the discipline of the mind. One learns little from such spectacle, but I confess the wine was better than the play.

I have secured a seat in the front coupé for our departure to Paris tomorrow. The journey will be long, and the heat oppressive, but I look forward to the movement. Do not worry for me; I am well enough to endure the dust and the noise.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: The day before, Hegel had travelled to Karlstein, an old castle with old paintings, about four hours away. In hot weather this morning he revisited churches and galleries, finishing his sightseeing. He lunched with the uncle's family, who then drove the party by carriage to a pleasure ground outside town. He was to dine with them again the next day.
X: Friday, September 17. Yesterday I spent the whole day on a trip to Carlstein, an old castle four hours from here, where old paintings still hang, but otherwise there is nothing to see; — this morning I visited the churches and galleries, partly repeating what I had seen before, and have finished my business, i.e., seeing the sights. Yesterday’s tour with its heat, as well as the heat this morning, had made me very weak and affected me; — lunch at Uncle’s house today restored me wonderfully. After the meal, Mr. O. took us by carriage to a very pleasant place of amusement — here all the foliage is still firm and green, although it has not rained for a long time. Tomorrow I shall dine with the same family again; I am very well with them and with their heartfelt, friendly reception...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The heat here in Prague is oppressive, a thick blanket that seems to press down upon the spirit. I spent this afternoon wandering the churches and galleries, seeking some coolness among the old paintings, yet the air remains heavy. It is a strange sensation, to be so far from our quiet Berlin evenings, walking alone through these crowded streets.

I had the pleasure of lunching with my host’s family today. They are a cheerful lot, and after the meal, we drove out to a pleasure ground on the outskirts. The carriage ride was dusty, but the fresh air did me good. I dine with them again tomorrow, so do not worry for my sustenance, only for my patience. I miss your company and the comfort of our home. The journey is long, but I am making my way.

Yours,
Hegel

card: After a day in Kassel with the Beers, Hegel took a hired coach to Marburg and briefly called on Suabedissen. In Wetzlar he spent an afternoon and evening with Schulz's family; next morning Schulz showed him the town and saw him onto the 10 a.m. mail coach. He reached Koblenz the previous day and took a bath before writing.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Koblenz yesterday, though the journey from Kassel was tedious enough. I dined with the Beers, then took a coach to Marburg, where I called briefly on Suabedissen. The heat was oppressive, and I was glad to spend the afternoon in Wetzlar with Schulz’s family. His kindness in showing me the town this morning, and seeing me onto the 10 a.m. mail coach, was a welcome respite from the dust and noise of travel.

I have taken a bath, which has done me good. The Rhine here is grand, but I confess the landscape does not stir the spirit quite as the city does. I miss the quiet of our home and the presence of the boys. I hope this letter finds you and the children well. Do not worry too much about my pace; I am taking things as they come.

Your affectionate,
Georg
Y: I have just come from the bath and am writing to you hastily, as the post leaves at 3 o'clock and lunch is approaching. — You can see from the date and the bath taken that I have already advanced about 80 miles and am taking my cure very seriously. — I have first to give you the further report of my journey, which is rather simple. Mr. and Mde Beer will have already told you, before receiving this letter, about the pleasant day we spent together in Cassel, despite the bad weather... The express post only left Cassel on Tuesday evening, so I traveled with a hired coach on Monday the 21st from Cassel to Marburg — without any noteworthy incident; in the evening I was still able to visit Hofrath Suabedissen, Professor of Philosophy, in that bumpy little nest, but he had a whole hedge of female relatives with him, so that I set off again immediately. On Tuesday I drove to Wetzlar, where I first visited Schulz, who lives outside the city in the garden, after dinner; he and his wife had a heartfelt joy over my visit; they are all very healthy and looking well — the children, my godchildren, who were almost sickly, are all very strong and well; the garden is on a hill, and has some buildings lying about 30 steps up the slope; I had to stay with him in the afternoon and evening until 10 o'clock. In the morning Schulz came to me, showed me around the little that was worth seeing, and stayed with me until I boarded the express post at 10 o'clock. — He is with body and soul engaged in very interesting studies; his conversation was very instructive to me; the whole family lives quite happily... Yesterday I arrived in Koblenz at 10 o'clock; the express post from there to Trier leaves already tomorrow; that was too early; I will therefore only depart with it on Monday, — to Trier in one day. Had I been able to calculate it, I could have asked you to write to me in Trier, where I — and that on my birthday — could have received a letter from you; I will drink to your well-being and happiness on that occasion. — Now a heartfelt kiss and greeting, likewise to the boys. In Paris I no longer understand German. — Write to me a lot from Berlin — about you and other things... Greet the friends, Privy Councillor Schulze in particular.

card: Hegel had attended a three-act ballet in Paris about a sleepwalker who is found asleep in a nobleman's bedroom and later seen crossing a roof with a lantern; only the first act was danced, the rest mimed. On the previous day he visited Saint-Cloud, on the Seine outside Paris.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I hope the children are well and that Karl is not too absorbed in his studies tonight. I write from Paris, where the air is thick with September damp.

Yesterday I took a carriage to Saint-Cloud. The Seine was grey and sluggish, but the view from the terrace was grand enough to remind me that nature, however beautiful, lacks the inner movement of Spirit.

Tonight, however, I sat through a three-act ballet on a sleepwalker. It was absurd. The hero is found in a nobleman’s bed, then mimes crossing a roof with a lantern. Only the first act was actually danced; the rest was mere pantomime. The audience laughed, but I felt only a profound irritation. To see human freedom reduced to such mechanical, dream-like posturing is painful. It is a spirit asleep, yet it does not even have the dignity of true slumber.

I miss our walks in the Tiergarten. Pray send my regards to Ludwig.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: What is there to say about the ballet? — a subject that no one has yet thought to treat in a ballet, and which would hardly occur to anyone else — namely, a sleepwalker. In the first act, there is dancing — with all its complications; yet there is a plot. Grace, cheerfulness, agility (the corps de ballet has it too!); in the second act, a sleepwalker appears, coming through the window on a ladder with a lantern in her hand, into the master of the house’s bedroom, lies down — after having knelt and prayed (the French around me said she was a Protestant, since it is not a church in which she prays; Protestant churches are officially called temples here). — The master — out of reverence — climbs out of the same window and leaves her alone — great applause for this virtuous behavior. The third act begins with the greatest anger of the sleepwalker’s fiancé, that she was found sleeping in a gentleman’s room. The gentleman explains to him and to the entire audience that she came into his room as a sleepwalker; they do not want to comprehend or understand it; then she appears once more on the roof, strolling with the lantern and marching down from a high, dangerously collapsed wall; — reconciliation ends everything. — In the last two acts, there is no more dancing — but much grace and liveliness in the pantomime, which admittedly cannot be understandable everywhere. — Yesterday I was in St. Cloud — beautiful surroundings — on the bank of the Seine, whose curves here form almost a complete circle, enclosing the vineyard hill; before one lies Paris with its beautiful towers and domes and countless houses. —

card: The spell of fair weather in Vienna ended. That morning the Kleins left the city; during their stay they and Hegel had done little sightseeing together but had met at meals. Hegel planned to remain a few more days to see places he had not yet visited.
X: The fine weather is now past, but the pleasant days in Aranjuez are not quite over, for I shall spend a few more here; there is still much that I do not know. But to consider this, and what I already know, more exhaustively, a few weeks would certainly not have been enough. — This morning the Kleins are leaving from here; although it was hardly possible for us to go about and see things together much, we did see each other at table, and it was a very pleasant company.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The long spell of fair weather has finally broken. The air feels different tonight, a bit heavier, as if the city is settling in for a proper autumn. The Kleins departed this morning. Our time together was brief and largely confined to our meals; we did little sightseeing, which I confess I found rather convenient. I prefer the company of good food and conversation to wandering the streets in the heat, though I suspect you would have enjoyed the promenades.

I intend to stay a few more days. There are places I have not yet visited, and now that the oppressive heat has lifted, I feel I can actually walk again without feeling like a boiled egg. I shall take my time, perhaps visit the museum properly, and enjoy a quiet evening with a glass of wine and a good book. Do not worry. I am comfortable, and the change in weather feels like a relief.

Yours affectionately,

G.

card: In the evening Hegel attended Mozart's Marriage of Figaro, performed by the Italian company: Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Susanna, Dardanelli as the Countess and Donzelli as the Count. His seat was nearer the stage than on his first visit. The Kleins had extended their stay over Sunday to attend this performance.
X: To bring this to a close, I was in the evening—where?—at Mozart’s *The Marriage of Figaro*. The Kleins stayed on Sunday for that reason. I had to admit to myself that the Italian voices in this more restrained music did not seem to have as much opportunity to develop their brilliant runs, which had been so sweet to hear; but in themselves, with what perfection were the arias, duets, etc., especially the recitatives, delivered—the latter are entirely the artist’s own natural creations. Lablache, what a Figaro! Fodor as Susanna—she would indeed have had to be more beautiful and taller for this role. Signora Dardanelli as the Countess; I sat closer to the stage this time than the first time I saw her—what a beautiful woman, a lovely Italian head, and a calmness, nobility in posture and action—very lovely, beautiful decorum—I almost fell into your situation and would have fallen in love with this woman! She is in fact most charming. Donzelli as the Count—compared rather unfavorably to her; such situations are not good for him.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with dust and music, but I am well. Tonight, the Kleins kept their word, and we sat closer to the stage than before. The Italian company performed Figaro, and I must confess, the proximity changed everything. I did not merely hear the drama; I felt the tension of the characters’ fates pressing in. Lablache’s Figaro was a whirlwind of wit, while Dardanelli’s Countess held a stillness that was almost painful to watch. The music was not just heard; it was a movement of the spirit, resolving into a freedom that felt tangible. It is a reminder that art, like the state, is the actuality of the ethical idea made visible. We are exhausted but content. The journey is long, but moments like this make the road bearable. I miss your quiet presence at home.

Your devoted,
Georg

card: Hegel was going back to the Louvre gallery on its last open day before an exhibition of living painters, to meet Raumer and Panofka, whom he had met there the previous day; some days earlier he had walked through it with Cousin. At the Théâtre-Français he had seen Alzire, L'École des maris, and Emilia with Mlle Mars and Mlle Leverd.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The Louvre closed its doors to us today, the last night before the living artists take over. It was strange, walking through that silence with Raumer and Panofka, knowing the walls belong to history now, not just the present. I saw Alzire and L’École des maris earlier; Mlle Mars is still magnificent, though time has added a weight to her voice that suits the tragedy.

I find myself thinking of our sons. I hope they are not merely playing at freedom, but learning the discipline that makes judgment possible. A child who is not taught to obey will never know the true dignity of doing what is right. I miss our evenings, the cards, the quiet. The air here is thick with expectation, but I am tired.

Tell the boys their father is well, and that he loves them.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: The painting gallery is in the Louvre, — a straight, long hall, vaulted at the top — both sides hung with paintings; — a passage, almost endless, a quarter of an hour long; I had gone through it quickly with Cousin a few days ago, yesterday I wanted to begin the more thorough studies or views, when it turned out that exactly yesterday and today there is still time, — from tomorrow the museum (i.e. the collection of paintings and also the antiquities) is closed for preparation for the painting exhibition of current masters; — there is a great wealth and famous pieces by the noblest masters, which one has seen a hundred times in engravings, present; — by Raphael, Correggio, Leon. da Vinci, Titian and so on, — I am going back again in half an hour, to find Raumer!) and Panofka, whom I met there yesterday, and to make an appointment with them for this afternoon, it is Sunday and church fair in St. Cloud (i.e. fishing in Stralau)?) ; Cousin advises against going; instead there is horse racing at the Champ de Mars. — Raumer has an audience with Mlle Mars today at noon; he must be with all the actresses); Cousin finds it ridiculous to go to her, — to Talma or Mde Pasta, — if they were still here — he would have taken me. By the way Mlle Mars; in the theater I have of course also already been — in the French one twice, — once Alzire by Voltaire and l'école des maris by Moliere — so from the most famous pieces, — the other time in Emilia, tragedy after W. Scott, — an Emilia has Mlle Mars, — then Mlle Leverd (Queen Elizabeth) played, — especially the Mars very charming and noble, of course with peculiarity; one understands Mlle Mars and Leverd every word 7); they play, as the men in general also, much more restrained, with much less pathetic raging than our actors and actresses, — the men are mediocre, Lafond the most famous after Talma, almost like a butcher; — the French are generally calmer and more definite in expressing their feelings than we are, especially you; how often do I say to you, you should say and treat the matter without feeling, yet your liveliness often suits you quite nicely!

card: Hegel and his companions drove to an abattoir and also saw the Bourse, Montmartre, which overlooks the city, and the palace of the Chamber of Deputies. At 5:30 p.m. he dined with Cousin and Fauriel, editor of the modern Greek folk songs. Some days earlier he had dined with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis and Fauriel.
X:
My dearest Marie,

Paris keeps its promise. We drove to the abattoir today; the machinery of death here is as organized as life, a stark reminder of necessity. We also visited the Bourse, where money dances, and Montmartre, from which the city stretches out like a vast, breathing body. The Palace of the Deputies stands firm, a symbol of the ethical state actualized in law.

Dinner was lively with Cousin and Fauriel. Fauriel’s Greek folk songs are charming, though he speaks of them as curiosities rather than the soul of a people. I have also enjoyed Mignet and Thiers; their history is sharp, though perhaps too much concerned with events and not enough with spirit.

I think of you and the boys constantly. The air is thick with history, but my heart remains in Berlin. Write soon.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.
Y: You notice that I do not write about Paris with such fire and enthusiasm as I did from Vienna, and that you have communicated much to the friends; that may be so, but everything I write is too fleeting to be capable of much communication. You must take into account that my ill health has caused me to lose much time, and then that everything is so enormously vast and sprawling that one must be externally quite vigorous to encompass more, and must stay here longer to come into deeper contacts and penetrations. It is a most interesting ground, but a few weeks are only enough to get out of the stupor and into the habit of all the brilliant and manifold things. Today, for example, we drove to an abattoir, i.e., a slaughterhouse—in which city in the world would I drive to a slaughterhouse?—but this is one of the curiosities that Paris owes to Napoleon, as it does to a hundred other great things. Then we were on the Montmartre, where one overlooks the wealth of houses in Paris and the splendid, fertile, lively surroundings; also in the Palace of the Chamber of Deputies. We saw the Stock Exchange, still laid out by Napoleon, beforehand, what a temple! At half past six o’clock I dined with Cousin and Fauriel (the editor of the Greek songs, which have also been translated into German). A few days ago we dined together with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis, Fauriel, and so on; in short, one must be in Paris for half a year to become more familiar with everything for which one takes a deeper interest, and, as said, through habit to lose all interest in what is striking and worth seeing for the first period. Cousin has often laughed at me when I saw and found remarkable what the conscience of a traveler and the Manual of the Foreigner prescribed to see.

card: In the evening, after writing to his wife, Hegel took the coach to Breda. There he viewed a tomb monument ascribed to Michelangelo, showing a count and his wife in alabaster lying on a black slab, while four standing figures, among them Julius Caesar, Hannibal and Regulus, support a second slab above them at the corners.
X: That evening, after I had written to you, I took the carriage to Breda, where I saw the magnificent work by Michelangelo—a mausoleum. Six life-sized figures of white alabaster: a count and his wife, lying in death, and four figures: Julius Caesar, Hannibal, Regulus, and a warrior standing bent over at the four corners of the black stone on which they lie, carrying on their shoulders a similar black stone—a magnificent, spirited work by the greatest master.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The light in The Hague is fading as I write. I take the coach to Breda tonight, though I confess the journey seems less a necessity than a whim for fresh air. The Dutch spirit is orderly, but I find myself craving the warmth of our home and the sound of the children’s voices.

I must tell you of a strange sight I passed today. A tomb monument, they say by Michelangelo. Alabaster figures of a count and his wife lie upon a black slab, yet above them stand four giants—Caesar, Hannibal, Regulus—holding up the stone. It struck me as a terrible image of history: the dead held aloft by the weight of past empires, while the living are reduced to mere stone. It made me think of how our own freedom is not a gift from nature, but a struggle carried on by the spirits of ages.

I miss you terribly. The wind is rising, and I feel the need for your steadying presence.

Your devoted,
G.
